title: Seeing Him
hookLine: the believers will see their Lord as they see the moon

lines: A FULL MOON, A CIRCLE OF FRIENDS.
cards: Night. A group of companions is sitting with the Prophet, peace be upon him, and the moon is full. The companion Jarir ibn Abdullah remembers what came next.
The Prophet looked at it and spoke. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Jarir reports it: you will see your Lord as you see this moon, and you will have no trouble seeing Him.
A whole crowd under one moon, and nobody pushing for a better look.

teach.h: THE MOON: CLEAR, AND SEEN BY ALL.
teach.b: Why the moon? Look at the hadith's own words: no trouble seeing Him. A full moon is one thing, and everyone sees it at once.
Nobody stands in line; nobody blocks anyone's view. The comparison is about the seeing, clear and shared, not about Allah being like the moon, and Muslim teachers are careful on that point.
The Qur'an speaks of the same hope.
In Pickthall's translation: "That day will faces be resplendent, Looking toward their Lord."
Here the theologians from earlier in this block return, because this was one of their real questions. Another verse says vision does not grasp Him, while He grasps all vision. How do the two fit?
The Ash'ari and Maturidi schools, and the Athari approach, affirm that the believers will truly see their Lord in the hereafter, without asking how.

The Mu'tazilah held that Allah is not seen with the eyes, and read the verses about seeing another way. Twelver Shia theology, too, holds that He is not seen with physical eyes, and speaks of a seeing of the heart.
Each side reads both verses. What they share is the hope of nearness to Allah. And that gives these unseen days a direction.

teach.h: A FACE TURNED TOWARD ITS LORD.
teach.b: Not only escape from the fire or a stay in the garden, but a face turned toward its Lord.

how: Sunni Muslims (Ash'ari, Maturidi and Athari) affirm that believers will see their Lord in the hereafter without asking how, citing this hadith and Qur'an 75:22–23; the Mu'tazilah and Twelver Shia theologians hold that Allah is not seen with physical eyes and read these texts differently.

o: a vision of the Prophet that comes to the pious in dreams
the first sighting of the new moon that begins Ramadan
the hope of seeing Allah in the hereafter, clear as the moon

p: reported the hadith of the moon
a seeing of the heart, not the eyes

s: the hadith says Allah is like the moon
it compares the seeing, clear and shared, not Allah Himself.
Muslim theologians have answered the question of seeing Allah in different ways
Ash'ari, Maturidi and Athari affirm it without asking how; the Mu'tazilah and Twelver Shia read it otherwise.
the companions were sitting under a full moon when the Prophet said it
Jarir reports the Prophet looked at the moon and said: as you see this moon.

games.q: you're a theologian. one verse says the faces look toward their Lord; another says vision does not grasp Him. what do you do?
o: read the two together, in your school's way.
say the question can't be asked.
games.why: every school kept both verses; they differed on how the two fit, and some added: without asking how.

practice: If the moon is out, go and look at it, full or not; if it's day, or cloudy, or you're indoors, picture a full moon you remember, round and bright over a dark street.

Notice how it looks the same to everyone under it, and let the hadith come to mind: as you see this moon. If you pray, hold the hope of that seeing in silence; if not, rest in the plain wonder of the light.

wordCard.voice: Seeing Him. The hope that the believers will see their Lord in the hereafter, as clearly as a crowd sees the full moon. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: seeing, vision; the theologians' word for the seeing of Allah.

carryVoice: Your line: like seeing the moon. Clear, and shared by everyone under it. See you tomorrow.
